query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A minor substitutional addition of chromium (≈4–5 at%) to (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 will induce the controlled precipitation of a reticulated, ductile secondary phase that interrupts the continuous brittle matrix, thereby enhancing mechanical integrity without significantly compromising the large caloric response.
generation.material_initial_state: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 exhibits a large caloric effect (magnetocaloric/barocaloric) but suffers from poor structural integrity and cracking due to a continuous brittle phase.
generation.intervention: Introduce approximately 4–5 atomic percent Cr into the alloy composition via substitution for one of the constituent elements.
generation.conditions: The modified alloy should be processed under the same thermal and field-cycling conditions used for caloric testing (e.g., under moderate applied magnetic or pressure fields and typical operating temperatures) and evaluated under quasi-static mechanical loading regimes.
generation.structural_mediator: The Cr addition is expected to trigger the formation of finely dispersed, ductile secondary (likely Laves-type) precipitates that form along grain boundaries or within the microstructure, effectively breaking the continuity of the brittle phase.
generation.mechanism: Chromium, as a potent alloying element, shifts phase equilibria toward the precipitation of a discrete ductile secondary phase. This phase formation reduces the connectivity of the brittle matrix, enhances dislocation mobility, and mitigates crack propagation while preserving the magnetostructural transition responsible for the caloric response.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Cr-doped alloy will show a significant improvement in mechanical integrity (e.g., ~20–30% increase in strength and higher fracture strain) while retaining at least 90% of the original caloric entropy change.
generation.baseline: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 without Cr displays high caloric performance but has poor mechanical robustness and is prone to cracking.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected under typical caloric operating conditions (applied fields, cycling temperatures) and with controlled processing parameters; significant deviations in processing or composition may alter phase stability and the balance between caloric and mechanical properties.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimal Cr concentration and processing conditions needed to achieve the best balance between enhanced mechanical integrity and maintained caloric response are uncertain, as the interplay between precipitate morphology and the caloric transition requires careful tuning.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of alloys using identical processing: one set of the baseline (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 and a second set where ~4–5 at% Cr is substituted into the composition. Conduct microstructural characterization (using TEM/SEM) to verify the formation of a discrete secondary precipitate phase and perform mechanical testing (tensile and compression) together with caloric cycling tests (magnetocaloric or barocaloric measurements) under the same applied field and temperature regimes.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Cr-containing alloy does not exhibit at least a ~15% improvement in mechanical integrity (e.g., strength or ductility) without a reduction of the caloric entropy change by more than 10% relative to the baseline alloy, then the hypothesis is refuted.

Question: How does the addition of Cr to the HfMoTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy affect its phase composition, microstructure, and room-temperature mechanical properties, specifically regarding the synergy between strength and ductility?. System: HfMoTaTiZr (30.0 at% Hf, 16.1 at% Mo, 30.4 at% Ta, 8.1 at% Ti, 15.4 at% Zr) and HfMoTaTiZrCr0.5 (28.8 at% Hf, 15.5 at% Mo, 29.1 at% Ta, 7.7 at% Ti, 14.7 at% Zr, 4.2 at% Cr). Processing: Vacuum arc melting in an inert gas atmosphere; ingots re-melted at least 5 times to improve chemical homogeneity; weight loss did not exceed 0.5 wt%. Test conditions: Room temperature; Vickers hardness with 0.3 kg load and 15 s dwelling time; compression tests on cylindrical samples (3 mm diameter, 6 mm height) at a ram speed of 0.008 mm s−1 (strain rate 0.001/s).
